newsitem.title: USA: Disaster underscores desperation in Haiti - experts.
newsitem.headline: Disaster underscores desperation in Haiti - experts.

text.p: A report that 180 Haitian boat people may have died this month trying to reach Florida focused attention on Thursday on desperate living conditions in the Caribbean island.

Experts said the incident, which remained unconfirmed, underscored the grinding poverty that continues to dominate Haitian life, in spite of two years of international intervention that began in 1994, when U.S.-led troops occupied the country and restored freely elected President Jean-Bertrand Aristide to power.

On Thursday, Haitian government officials, police and U.N. workers were trying to unearth information about the "Angel Gabriel," a 60-foot (20-meter) wooden sailboat that witnesses said left the southern port city of Petit-Goave on Nov. 3 crammed with some 180 people.

The overcrowded ship headed for Florida, but was not heard from again. News of its departure emerged on Wednesday, when Haiti's Radio Metropole reported that relatives of people who had been on board the craft attempted to lynch the couple who reportedly arranged the trip.

One woman who said she had boarded the boat and then decided it was too crowded, told Reuters there were about 40 children among the 180 people on board and that the refugees had paid $100 each for passage.

Haitian government officials Thursday declined comment on the reports or speculation that continuing grinding poverty was prompting dangerous, illegal immigration in spite of the installation of a freely elected government.
"I cannot comment on something about which I have no information," a Foreign Ministry official said.
The Haitian government, under President Rene Preval, Aristide's successor, has been unable to combat poverty and has made only very slow movement toward privatisation and other economic reform.
Haiti is the poorest country in the hemisphere, with an estimated $270 annual per capita income, illiteracy rate of more than 70 percent and widespread unemployment.

And though a freely elected government has been in place since 20,000 U.S.-led troops occupied the country two years ago, ending a violent three-year military dictatorship, there has been no appreciable improvement in the nation's economy.
"It is always a country of people fleeing," said Ken Boodhoo, a professor at Florida International University in Miami who runs a foundation supporting grass roots development in Haiti.
"Because the people need help now, immediately. And the kinds of programmes you are putting into place cannot deliver in the short term."

Robert Rotberg, a Harvard University professor and president of the World Peace Foundation, said, "Preval's government has not managed to get things moving as fast as everyone had hoped. It may not be his fault at all, but it certainly has impacted on Haitian expectations on what is going to happen this winter."

The U.S. Coast Guard, which said it had no knowledge of the missing boat, has seen no increase in Haitian boat people. Although Coast Guard cutters and ships regularly patrol the Caribbean, no Haitians had been picked up at sea in November, and only 35 were picked up in October.
In contrast, 235 were intercepted in March, 179 in February and 195 in January, said a spokesman in Miami. In 1995, 1,969 Haitians were intercepted at sea.
In contrast, 24,917 were picked up in 1994, most during the months of dictatorship and international embargo that preceeded Aristide's return.
Almost all of the Haitians picked up by the Coast Guard are returned to their homeland.
